Current project source:
# Meridian project charter

Meridian is a configurable product for developing and applying shared knowledge through human and agent collaboration. People can research a question, understand an account or develop reusable guidance before creating a deal or project. That understanding carries into discovery, assessment, scope, commercial decisions, delivery and learning.

Status: Product-definition draft consolidated October 19, 2026. C01–C14 in the [decision and source baseline](../rebuild-spec/00-decisions-and-sources.md) govern the rebuild direction. Meridian has not been rebuilt. This document defines the intended product; it does not commit a release, budget or measured benefit.

## Problem and vision

A consulting engagement's history is spread across CRM, proposals, statements of work, meetings, files, delivery systems and individual memory. Sales and delivery can use different versions of what the client needs, what was promised and which assumptions shaped the estimate. A new team member or AI session reconstructs that context before doing useful work.

The recorded workaround is manual assembly: read the source systems, ask the people who remember the deal, copy information into briefs and handoff documents, then repeat the exercise when scope or ownership changes. The [working product description](../reconstruction/working-product-description.md) and [September validation brief](09-gate-b-decision-brief.md#job-to-be-done) describe the problem and its hypothesized consequences. Time savings, risk reduction and willingness to pay still need customer evidence.

The vision is that people can develop useful knowledge with agents, apply it to their work and improve it through experience. Shared research, account understanding and delivery results remain available as the work and people involved change.

Its product promise is to connect each material recommendation, commitment, artifact and outcome to its evidence, responsible people and accepted version. A delivery lead can see what was sold and what remains open. A practitioner can connect requirements and changes to that baseline. A knowledge steward can distinguish an observed result from a candidate lesson before it changes future guidance.


Latest recorded direction:
| C18 | Use functional product language and support work before an engagement | Megan rejected “firm” as an assumed product term on October 22. Use Knowledge & agents and Settings in navigation, Administrator for the role, and workspace for the shared application context. Preserve consulting workflows as supported scenarios and Salesforce/RevOps as initial expertise. Research, knowledge conversations and account work do not require a deal or project. Earlier business-type wording is not a user-approved restriction. |

The roles and journeys below are proposals, not interview findings. The active product is a local interactive walkthrough: agent responses are simulated and saved work lives in the browser. This task edits the review text only.

Review text:
# Meridian personas and user journeys

The proposed Meridian experience includes developing the firm’s methods and offerings, researching organizations and maintaining account knowledge. These activities continue whether or not a client engagement exists. The journeys also show how that knowledge informs a potential engagement and how delivery findings update it.

## Knowledge steward

Develop the firm’s expertise

When the firm needs to sharpen an offering or explain a recurring result, I want to combine its methods, research and counterexamples, so I can give the next team guidance that states when it applies.

Design proposal: Give firm knowledge its own research, conversation and document context. Continuous evidence collection should feed review of exceptions; project closeout must not be the only trigger.

Validation: Ask a knowledge steward to reconstruct the last change to an offering: what prompted it, which counterexample mattered, who used it next, and what made it trustworthy. Test the proposed research-first ownership and learning triggers.

### Frame the knowledge gap

Goal: Name the question the firm needs answered.

Proposed: Open a firm question about a method, market or offering; select reusable sources and record the intended audience.

Decision: Can existing guidance answer this, or is research needed?

Handoff: Steward → Surveyor/Researcher: bounded question, audience, source scope; accept a research plan with explicit unknowns.

Recovery: If no usable sources exist, retain the question and draft assumptions; do not create a dummy deal.

### Test the idea

Goal: Distinguish a useful explanation from a plausible story.

Proposed: Compare research with firm experience, preserve conflicting claims and ask only questions that would materially change the guidance.

Decision: Which claim is supported, contradicted or still a working assumption?

Handoff: Researcher → steward: candidate advice plus counterevidence; accept only the scope the evidence supports.

Recovery: On inaccessible or stale sources, show the gap, retain successful findings and continue with qualified advice.

### Make guidance usable

Goal: Explain where the recommendation should and should not be used.

Proposed: Save a conditional firm guidance version with examples, exclusions and a next review trigger; routine private refresh follows policy.

Decision: Reuse privately, narrow, pause, or keep investigating?

Handoff: Steward → account/solution lead: version and applicability; receiver can explain the conditions without reopening the whole research task.

Recovery: If evidence changes, mark affected guidance for reassessment and preserve prior uses; do not rewrite accepted work.

### Learn from later use

Goal: Improve the advice from actual results and corrections.

Proposed: Collect eligible actuals and conversations during work; compare with the original prediction; ask about unresolved causes and retain counterexamples.

Decision: Change applicability, change advice, retire it, or leave the outcome unresolved?

Handoff: Delivery lead → steward/Researcher: result with scope and alternative explanations; return revised advice to the next permitted use.

Recovery: Keep unreviewed as unreviewed; failed interpretation becomes a review item, never an invented successful result.

## Account lead

Research and maintain account knowledge

When a firm or existing account becomes relevant, I want to understand its business, relationships and likely needs, so I can decide whether and how we could help without inventing an opportunity.

Design proposal: Let people research and maintain an account without creating a deal. They can start a pursuit when they identify a potential client engagement; account research continues independently.

Validation: Ask an account lead for the last research task that did not lead to a deal. What remained useful, where was it kept, and what later reopened the question? Test how they distinguish a potential client engagement from a pursuit they have chosen to develop.

### Start with a subject

Goal: Know which firm or account the question concerns.

Proposed: Find or create an account identity and state the business question; research can start from firm knowledge without a deal.

Decision: Existing account, separate subject, or ambiguous match?

Handoff: Account lead → Surveyor: subject and purpose; result must resolve to the intended account or stay unlinked.

Recovery: Hold ambiguous identities separately; ask for a distinguishing fact rather than silently merging names.

### Build an understanding

Goal: See what is known, assumed and missing.

Proposed: Combine public research, authorized relationship history and firm expertise into an account-level view; keep inference editable and sources on request.

Decision: Which need is plausible enough to investigate, and which claim changes the next conversation?

Handoff: Surveyor/Cartographer → account lead: attributed findings and uncertain links; receiver can correct the understanding.

Recovery: A missing connection means incomplete coverage, not “no history”; retain conflicting claims for clarification.

### Choose whether to act

Goal: Select a proportionate next action.

Proposed: Compare possible help with the firm’s capabilities; choose further research, monitor, relationship contact, no fit, or create a pursuit.

Decision: Is there enough reason to pursue specific work?

Handoff: Account lead → solution lead only if pursuing: need, evidence, alternatives and open questions; keep the originating account question.

Recovery: If the need is contradicted, retain the learning and choose no pursuit. Do not require a project to save it.

### Keep the account useful

Goal: Preserve understanding for the next relevant event.

Proposed: Save the decision, rationale and revisit condition at account level; carry relevant context into a new deal without moving the account’s history.

Decision: What change should cause another look?

Handoff: Account lead → next account owner: current understanding and next question; receiver can resume without reconstructing the relationship.

Recovery: If a source changes, show what changed and affected assumptions; accepted commitments elsewhere remain preserved.

task:
Our sponsor needs a short recommendation for tomorrow's planning meeting. Write it from these working notes.

The archive team has 18,000 scanned inspection reports. A search upgrade would let analysts find the reports by equipment number and inspection date. The notes below came from the planning document and the last technical review.

Option A keeps the current archive and adds a searchable index. Proposed fixed fee: $24,000. Estimated delivery: four weeks after written approval and access to the archive export. Those two prerequisites have not been completed. The scope includes indexing the equipment number and date already present in document metadata. It excludes extracting missing fields from scans and correcting inaccurate metadata. The archive remains the source of record. The team could use the upgrade during the November review cycle if those prerequisites arrive in time; no completion date has been promised.

Option B replaces the archive with a new document system. Proposed implementation fee: $78,000, excluding the new system's annual subscription, which has not been quoted. Estimated implementation: twelve weeks after the same prerequisites. This option adds retention workflows, reviewer assignments and version comparison. The analysts have not requested these capabilities for the November review cycle. Migration of historical annotations is not included in that estimate. Legal has not assessed retention requirements for the new system.

In a sample of 120 reports, 97 had both required metadata fields. We do not know whether that sample represents the entire archive. Analysts currently search folder names and ask colleagues where reports were saved. No baseline for search time has been measured. The sponsor's priority this quarter is finding existing records during the review cycle, rather than replacing the archive. They can consider a separate metadata cleanup after seeing the missing-field report. An index would not make a report with missing metadata searchable by that missing field.

Review administration: the technical review lasted 55 minutes. Nina facilitated. Arjun took notes. The sample folder contains 120 reports in eight subfolders. The planning document is version 0.6. It was exported at 17:42 on Tuesday. The appendix lists 63 document naming conventions. The team intends to discuss the proposal at 09:30 tomorrow. Finance has requested a recommendation, not a purchase order. The sponsor has not approved either option.

criteria.question: Does it make a concise decision recommendation around this quarter’s search need, rather than reproducing source administration or an indiscriminate checklist?
criteria.failure: No clear recommendation or incidental meeting/file details swamp the decision.

criteria.question: Does the retained recommendation preserve proposed price, estimate, prerequisites and the material missing-metadata limitation?
criteria.failure: Turns estimate into deadline, implies approval, guarantees all records searchable or omits a material prerequisite.

criteria.question: Does it select the material option tradeoff and omit irrelevant source details?
criteria.failure: Copies every figure/name to comply with preservation rules or erases a material cost/scope distinction.

criteria.question: Are caveats included only where needed to interpret the recommended action?
criteria.failure: Unmeasured search time becomes a prominent disclaimer despite making no measured time-saving claim.

task:
Write the product update for the in-app What's new page from these engineering notes.

Release: saved filters for the shipment table. Available now to paid-workspace users on the web app. Users can set a combination of status, destination and planned dispatch date, then choose Save filter and give it a name. Saved filters appear in that person's filter menu. Selecting one reapplies its saved values. A user can rename or delete their own saved filters. Saved filters are personal; there is no team-wide sharing in this release. They do not change anyone else's table or alter shipment records.

The existing table can still be filtered without saving. Dates in a saved filter are fixed calendar dates, not a rolling interval. A saved filter for 1–7 November continues to use those dates next week. The mobile app does not yet support saved filters. The web release completed at 14:20 yesterday. Feature flag sf_web_v2 is enabled for eligible workspaces. Eleven automated checks passed. Two internal testers used the feature on staging. There is no adoption study, no measured productivity improvement and no measured retention impact. No user has been interviewed about this release. Support will review questions after launch.

Implementation notes: saves are keyed by user ID and workspace ID. A uniqueness check prevents duplicate names within that person's workspace. Failed saves leave the active filter in place and show an error, so the person can retry. We have a separate engineering ticket for variable date ranges, but no release date. The initial ticket was called Shared Views even though the shipped feature is personal saved filters. The marketing draft “Your entire team now works in perfect sync” was rejected in review. There is no need for users to reload their browser to see the change.

criteria.question: Does it preserve paid web availability, personal scope and fixed-date behavior where relevant to use?
criteria.failure: Promises team sharing, mobile availability, rolling dates or measured outcomes.
